title: Masquerading: Break Process Trees
summary: Break process trees covers attempts to detach running code from the process that started it, so that parent-child relationships used by endpoint detection no longer link the payload to its launcher. On Linux the classic patterns are a double fork followed by the parent exiting, leaving the payload reparented to the init process, and the daemon system call, which detaches and runs the code in the background; on Windows the equivalent idea is arriving with an externally supplied parent process identifier so that the visible parent is unrelated to the real launcher. The behaviour itself leaves traces in process creation telemetry only if that telemetry records the true creator. Detection therefore focuses on correlation and gaps: a recorded parent process that never created the child, a parent process identifier that no longer exists or belongs to a different user, missing intermediate processes between a service or shell and a long-running payload, and unusual binary paths or arguments under init or another session leader. Legitimate daemons and service managers detach in similar ways, so the discriminator is the payload's identity, its arguments and its timing relative to the rest of the intrusion.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker makes a running program forget which program started it. Every program on a computer has a parent, the thing that launched it. Attackers can break that link. The program then looks like it appeared on its own.
beginner.whyItMatters: Security tools follow the chain of who started what. A broken chain removes the evidence that links the payload to the attacker. The tool may see a harmless program with no history. This makes it harder to spot the intrusion. Investigators must then work from other data.
howItWorks: The attacker already runs a small helper program on the machine.
That helper starts the real payload as a new process.
On Linux the helper can fork twice and then exit immediately.
The payload is then adopted by the very first system process and loses its link.
Another option is the daemon call, which detaches the program to run in the background.
Monitoring that only follows parent and child links sees a broken chain.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk that writes down who sent each visitor. A visitor slips in behind a porter, and the porter leaves the building. The desk has no record of who let the visitor in. Only the visitor's own badge gives a clue.
takeaways: Parent and child links are the base of most process monitoring.
A missing or impossible parent is itself a useful alert.
Correlate process creation logs with other evidence before you trust a chain.

objectives: Explain what a parent process and a process tree are.
Describe how double forking and detach style calls break the link.
State how this sub-technique differs from the parent masquerading technique.
Identify telemetry gaps that appear when a parent link is broken.
Compare suspicious detachment with normal daemon behaviour.
